This is an update of Spring & Summer events

> Spring events related to sensitivity/robustness analysis in different parts of the country.  Perhaps see you at one of them.
>

> Workshop "What Would it take to Change your Inference" at the Society for Research on Educational Effectiveness.

>   Where: Arlington Virginia. full description at the bottom of this email.
>   Register: You will be able to sign up at (might not be available yet): https://www.sree.org/spring-2020

> Talk and Discussion about Quantifying the Robustness of Inferences.
>   When: Thursday, March 19, TBD

https://msu.zoom.us/j/783760435 or come to room 128 Erickson Hall at Michigan State.

https://www.asanet.org/annual-meeting-2020/registration

> Ken
> [CHECK OUT http://konfound-it.com]

> Course Description
> What would it take to Change your Inference? Quantifying the Discourse about Causal Inferences in the Social Sciences <https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=http-3A__aefpweb.org_conferences_inference-2Dworkshop-23register&d=DwMFAg&c=nE__W8dFE-shTxStwXtp0A&r=F4oW3nXJKTAziDLTsgnr9A&m=tTgkUiXmiyzMSaXbIOq7Nc2xdpoXFG_tKfFuV3XYn2o&s=IFJjoTXJ_X8bmAfGWfD6NhSvkzHNct-UqzzjDRMOvzY&e=>
>
> Motivation
> Statistical inferences are often challenged because of uncontrolled bias. There may be bias due to uncontrolled confounding variables or non-random selection into a sample. We will answer the question about what it would take to change an inference by formalizing the sources of bias and quantifying the discourse about causal inferences in terms of those sources. For example, we will transform challenges such as “But the inference of a treatment effect might not be valid because of pre-existing differences between the treatment groups” to questions such as “How much bias must there have been due to uncontrolled pre-existing differences to make the inference invalid?” “QQQ% of the cases would have to be replaced with cases with no treatment effect to change the inference.”

When: Noon-4pm (eastern) on Wed March 11. Q&A available throughout, and extension from 4pm.-5pm.

Where: https://msu.zoom.us/j/783760435 <https://urldefense.com/v3/__http:/clicks.memberclicks-mail.net/ls/click?upn=Fqh5juu4mt8mQ-2Ff2BH2-2Bxg1VVJGeiR7LgoN0cf0AneQXAnA7YN6JGKPtyH5NB5Wuiada8O3VD3iXIk-2Bm-2Fa7VEYykE3CO-2FCgznX1JBackTE-2F1ho-2F6x9vTFuKEby3fH-2F-2Fmyi4a_Vhj2cCRnm6oZIsNjJN9jSU26oc62pA5anG-2F0hoZtqYqVmdWJS4eF3iVxOFgBAj-2FjWaYk4rYdkfUYeKvSXiG5b51BFYOxd-2FKtYV8izSd84z6k0ipKzMNRO6sPHGPCowigWC-2FIOi4ggNip7Fp-2BpBCDN1xvOBxcP0P5MKBbCCfJElLSZ8mrO6wGS2U2m8a7URXx4Pa2Omg3ATbzpgEt22E2EVeZceNXsE4njXGxR9YoxRTKz4y2U8hOO0yAcL1TOaPkzbIpxUZicqBu91VmerzGhaUxAW-2FNrV6-2Fr2aZ4CSMkuR7ekYbvLDri-2F5APkXqRucuWEJT6qQFavSGB-2BDK-2B6OKzg-3D-3D__;!!HXCxUKc!m4pbNox7qgKAXhmG_97CaDluPRh4x4xBbFzT5ff5Y6oD1zDOHhIgHfEmPwztqms$>

Materials: quick examples <https://msu.edu/~kenfrank/Quick%20Examples%20of%20Quantifying%20the%20Robustness%20to%20Invalidate.pptx> and powerpoint for combined frameworks <https://urldefense.com/v3/__http:/clicks.memberclicks-mail.net/ls/click?upn=Fqh5juu4mt8mQ-2Ff2BH2-2Bxg1VVJGeiR7LgoN0cf0AneQXAnA7YN6JGKPtyH5NB5Wuiada8O3VD3iXIk-2Bm-2Fa7VEYykE3CO-2FCgznX1JBackTE-2BVFuEz3lq2DN8-2BRs4Vk1OO90nj_Vhj2cCRnm6oZIsNjJN9jSU26oc62pA5anG-2F0hoZtqYqVmdWJS4eF3iVxOFgBAj-2FjWaYk4rYdkfUYeKvSXiG5b51BFYOxd-2FKtYV8izSd84z6k0ipKzMNRO6sPHGPCowigWC-2FIOi4ggNip7Fp-2BpBCDN1xvOBxcP0P5MKBbCCfJElIcKzoy6y-2BSGt3HvYx-2FBBF98-2Bt3h9yF6OPXHtE4CmzHh51iDRwA-2BRfGezjeHhu9bGs9oBRoa1RZ3nYXhcBiEPYeHoIbwlTBuCvqimw5lOrmjGT5BFJm3DhmyohKr5ui4PKpcPM5wVPvs00WJji4Ojeu2sWTQKNDu9C-2BfEuFJcUE2g-3D-3D__;!!HXCxUKc!m4pbNox7qgKAXhmG_97CaDluPRh4x4xBbFzT5ff5Y6oD1zDOHhIgHfEmsbIXCoI$>

Details:
What would it take to Change your Inference? Quantifying the Discourse about Causal Inferences in the Social Sciences

Motivation
Statistical inferences are often challenged because of uncontrolled bias. There may be bias due to uncontrolled confounding variables or non-random selection into a sample. We will answer the question about what it would take to change an inference by formalizing the sources of bias and quantifying the discourse about causal inferences in terms of those sources. For example, we will transform challenges such as “But the inference of a treatment effect might not be valid because of pre-existing differences between the treatment groups” to questions such as “How much bias must there have been due to uncontrolled pre-existing differences to make the inference invalid?” “QQQ% of the cases would have to be replaced with cases with no treatment effect to change the inference.”

Approaches
In part I we will use Rubin’s causal model to interpret how much bias there must be to invalidate an inference in terms of replacing observed cases with counterfactual cases or cases from an unsampled population. In part II, we will quantify the robustness of causal inferences in terms of correlations associated with unobserved variables or in unsampled populations. Calculations for bivariate and multivariate analysis will be presented using an app: http://konfound-it.com <https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=http-3A__konfound-2Dit.com_&d=DwMFAg&c=nE__W8dFE-shTxStwXtp0A&r=F4oW3nXJKTAziDLTsgnr9A&m=tTgkUiXmiyzMSaXbIOq7Nc2xdpoXFG_tKfFuV3XYn2o&s=vnvqy6IPjT-knVFXpuAZYm5IiApvS861BcbiLp3DgKA&e=> as well as macros in STATA and R and a spreadsheet for calculating indices [KonFound-it!].

Format
The format will be a mixture of presentation, individual exploration, and group work. Participants may include graduate students and professors, although all must be comfortable with basic regression and multiple regression. Participants should bring their own laptop, or be willing to work with another student who has a laptop. Participants may choose to bring to the course an example of an inference from a published study or their own work, as well as data analyses they are currently conducting.

 Ken

With all the changes floating around, this talk will now be virtual. Join on zoom if you like.

  When: Thursday, March 19, noon-1:30
  Where: on zoom. https://msu.zoom.us/j/783760435. Eric Dearing (Boston College) host.
  Slides: Quantifying What it Would Take to Change an Inference: Toward a Pragmatic Sociology (ASA Duncan lecture August 2018) <https://msu.edu/~kenfrank/Quantifying%20What%20it%20Would%20Take%20to%20Change%20an%20Inference%20--%20Toward%20a%20Pragmatic%20Sociology%20final.pptx>

Quantifying What it Would Take to Change an Inference: Toward a Pragmatic Social Science

Abstract

Pragmatic research informs the discrete choices of public policy, such as whether to implement a new policy or discontinue an old policy. This talk contributes to debates about policy by quantifying the strength of evidence relative to a threshold for making an inference.  In particular, we will generate statements such as “xx% of the estimated effect must be due to bias to invalidate the inference.”  Such statements can  be interpreted using a potential outcomes framework: “One would have to replace xx% of the cases with null hypothesis cases to invalidate the inference.” This type of statement allows researchers and policymakers to discuss the strength of evidence in terms of the conditions and contexts of people and organizations.  The  talk features a hands-on app: http://konfound-it.com. As well as commands in R and STATA available through the app.

Hope you are staying safe and sane.

Ken

Dear Dr. Frank,
Thank you so much for your generous offer of the workshop online!
I am a new assistant professor in applied psychology and have been learning the powerful KonFound-it app as well as the methods associated with it. It has been mind-opening. I registered for the workshop but got dragged out to a department meeting about the coronavirus response... It kills me to miss such a great opportunity as I was already dismayed to miss the SREE conference...
I was wondering if you could please share with me the recording of the workshop if available? My email is zhan...@umn.edu. I will keep it solely for my training purpose to protect your IP right.
Thank you so much for your help and support! May you have a wonderful weekend ahead!
Yanchen Zhang, PhD. NCSP.

messages.body_plain:
I teach sensitivity analysis as part of my course on regression.  I divide the standard workshop into two pieces.  Join us if you like.

What: course lectures: "what would it take to change your inference"
When: March 30 1-2:20 pm and April 1 1-2:20 p.m. eastern time.
Where: https://msu.zoom.us/j/783760435

abstract

Motivation

Statistical inferences are often
challenged because of uncontrolled bias.
There may be bias due to uncontrolled confounding variables or
non-random selection into a sample.  We will
answer the question about what it would take to change an inference by
formalizing the sources of bias and quantifying the discourse about causal
inferences in terms of those sources.
For example, we will transform challenges such as “But the inference of
a treatment effect might not be valid because of pre-existing differences
between the treatment groups” to questions such as “How much bias must there
have been due to uncontrolled pre-existing differences to make the inference
invalid?”

Approaches

In part I we will use Rubin’s
causal model to interpret how much bias there must be to invalidate an
inference in terms of replacing observed cases with counterfactual cases or
cases from an unsampled population. This generates
statements such as “One would have to replace qqq%
of the cases with cases with no effect to invalidate the inference.” In part
II, we will quantify the robustness of causal inferences in terms of
correlations associated with unobserved variables or in unsampled populations. This generates
statements such as “An omitted variable would have to be correlated at rrr with the treatment and outcome to
invalidate the inference.” Calculations for bivariate and multivariate analysis
will be presented using an app: http://konfound-it.com as well as macros in STATA and R
and a spreadsheet for
calculating indices [ <https://www.msu.edu/~kenfrank/KonFound-it!.xlsx>KonFound <https://www.msu.edu/~kenfrank/KonFound-it!.xlsx>-it!] <https://www.msu.edu/~kenfrank/KonFound-it!.xlsx>.

Format

The format will be a mixture of
presentation, individual exploration, and group work. Participants may include
graduate students and professors, although all must be comfortable with basic
regression and multiple regression. Participants should bring their own laptop, or be willing to work with another
student who has a laptop. Participants may choose to bring to the course an
example of an inference from a published study or their own work, as well as
data analyses they are currently conducting.

All related materials can be found at: https://msu.edu/~kenfrank/research.htm#causal
